Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re diving in, and yes, it can feel like a lot at first. Let’s keep it really simple.

Here are the main choices you’ll be making when you pick a rose:

Shape and size of the plant Think: what space do you want to fill?
Bush / shrub roses: Rounded plants, great for beds and borders. Many are repeat or continuous bloomers.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need support (fence, trellis, arch). Best if you want height or an archway.
Groundcover / landscape roses: Low, spreading plants for the front of beds or to spill over edges.

On our site, you can use filters like “bush,” “climbing,” or “groundcover” to narrow this.

Flower style This is about the look of the blooms.
Hybrid tea style: Classic “florist” look, usually one big flower per stem. Great for cutting.
Full, old-fashioned blooms: Lots of petals, very full, romantic look.
Simple / fewer petals: Open centers, often look a bit more wild or natural.

Product photos make this easy to see as you scroll.

Bloom pattern How often it blooms in a season:
Continuous bloomers: Keep flowers coming all season.
Repeat bloomers: Bloom in flushes with short rest periods in between.

The description on each rose will say if it is continuous or repeat blooming.

Sun and location
Full sun: At least 6 hours of direct sun per day. This is what most roses prefer.
Partial shade: About 4+ hours of sun. Only roses marked as shade tolerant will be happy here.

You can also set your hardiness zone at the top of the website so you only see roses that can handle your winters.

How you’ll plant it
In the ground: Best long term if you have garden space.
In a large container: Works well if you have a patio or deck. We ship all roses in 1-gallon containers; for long-term growing, you’ll move them into a larger pot or into the ground.

We only sell own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil, not bare root, so what you receive is a live potted plant ready to be planted within about 2 weeks of arrival.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question. Let’s keep it really simple and just talk about what to do the day your rose arrives.

I’ll assume you’re getting:

One potted rose
Maybe something like mint compost and/or Founders Fish Fertilizer

If you meant something else, tell me and I’ll adjust.

Timing and location
Plan to plant your rose within 2 weeks of arrival.
Only plant it in the ground after your last spring frost or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
All roses need to live outdoors, not indoors.

If you tell me your city or ZIP code, I can help you decide whether it’s better to plant in the ground now or slip it into a larger pot for a while.

Basic planting steps (first time) Whether you’re planting in the ground or a large pot, the core steps are similar:

Choose the spot

At least 6 hours of direct sun per day (full sun).
Soil that drains well and does not stay soggy.

Dig the hole

In the ground: about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep.
For a pot: choose at least a 10–15 gallon container for a bush rose, with drainage holes.

Prepare the soil

Mix your native soil with organic material such as compost. If you have mint compost, mix some into the top part of the backfill soil.

Remove the rose from its pot

Gently slide the rose out of the 1‑gallon container.
Loosen the outer roots lightly with your fingers if they are circling.

Set the rose in place

Place it so the base of the canes (where stems meet roots) sits at the same level it was in the pot.
Backfill around it with your prepared soil, pressing gently so there are no big air pockets.

Water deeply

Water slowly and thoroughly until the soil is soaked all the way through.

Mulch

Add a 1–2 inch layer of mulch, like mint compost, on top of the soil around the plant.
Keep mulch about 3 inches away from the base of the canes so they can breathe.
Mulch means a layer of material on top of the soil to hold moisture and protect roots.

How to use fertilizer the first time

For a beginner, gentle liquid feeding is safest.

If you have Founders Fish Fertilizer:

Wait until you see 4–6 inches of new growth and leaves.
Mix it with water exactly as the label directs.
Pour it onto the soil around the plant, not on dry soil; it is best when the soil is already slightly moist.
Repeat about every 4 weeks during the growing season in the first year.

Avoid strong granular fertilizers right at planting for a new rose in its first season. They can be a bit too intense for young roots.

Quick checklist for “first time use”
Keep rose outdoors.
Plant within 2 weeks.
Full sun if possible.
Water deeply 2–3 times per week at first (adjust if your weather is very hot or very cool).
Use mulch (like mint compost) on top of the soil.
Start liquid fertilizer only after it has started growing.
